candidateRows: The universe began to exist and therefore has a transcendent, immaterial, personal cause.
This cosmological argument directly supports the motion by inferring a personal creator from the universe's finite past.
Craig combines philosophical objections to an actual infinite past with cosmological evidence, then characterizes the required first cause as a personal mind.
Objective moral values and duties exist, and their existence requires God as their foundation.
The argument directly advances the motion by claiming that objective moral reality cannot be grounded under atheistic naturalism.
Craig contrasts evolved social behavior with objectively binding moral duties and argues that acknowledged instances of real evil entail God's existence.
The historical facts surrounding Jesus are best explained by his resurrection, which entails that God exists.
This argument directly supports the motion through an alleged divine miracle offered as the best explanation of specified historical claims.
Craig appeals to the empty tomb, reported appearances, and the disciples' transformed belief, rejecting naturalistic alternatives and inferring resurrection.
God cannot be disproved conclusively, but no feature of reality requires God and simpler explanations are available in principle.
This is Atkins's central burden against the motion and supplies the explanatory standard organizing all six of his subsequent lines of argument.
Atkins concedes logical possibilities involving God but argues that invoking an unlimited divine entity adds complexity and impedes explanatory inquiry.
An original universe may begin without a cause because causality and physical laws arise with the universe itself.
The move directly challenges the causal premise of Craig's cosmological argument and denies that a cosmic beginning presently requires divine agency.
Craig's claim that a universe beginning to exist must have a transcendent personal cause.
Atkins distinguishes daughter universes from an original universe, questions pre-universe causality, and treats scientific ignorance as no warrant for a creator.
Life-permitting constants do not require divine design because necessity or a multiplicity of universes can explain their values.
The argument blocks a major theistic design inference by presenting non-intentional alternatives for the universe's life-permitting physical parameters.
Atkins grants that the universe permits life but argues that constrained constants or varied constants across many universes remove any need for design.
There is no evidence that the universe has a purpose, so its existence supplies no basis for positing a purposeful God.
The move rejects teleological interpretation at the cosmic scale and thereby removes another proposed explanatory role for a personal deity.
Atkins characterizes cosmic purpose as an unwarranted projection of human purposes and says scientific explanation proceeds without detecting such purpose.
No reliable miracle has been established, and natural explanations are more credible than resurrection as an explanation of the reports.
This move directly contests Craig's historical argument by denying both reliable miracle evidence generally and the resurrection inference specifically.
Craig's claim that the historical facts concerning Jesus are best explained by a divine resurrection.
Atkins defines miracles as suspensions of natural law, denies reliable observations of them, and treats the resurrection sources and inference as unreliable.
Apparently gratuitous suffering is evidence against the existence of an all-loving God rather than a puzzle requiring theological reconciliation.
The evidential argument from evil directly opposes the motion by presenting widespread innocent suffering as more expected if no loving God exists.
Craig's theistic conclusion and his claim that real evil supports rather than undermines God's existence.
Atkins contrasts elaborate theodicies with the simpler hypothesis that no all-loving deity exists and treats suffering of innocents as contrary evidence.
Moral distinctions emerged through biological and social development, so morality does not require a divine source or judge.
The move directly contests the moral argument for God by proposing an evolutionary and social account of ethical behavior and moral regulation.
Craig's claim that objective moral values and duties cannot exist without God as their transcendent foundation.
Atkins locates moral behavior in evolutionary history, reflection on consequences, anthropology, and social stability rather than commands from a divine umpire.
The existence of evil is logically compatible with God if God could have morally sufficient reasons for permitting evil.
It directly answers a principal atheistic argument against God's existence and shifts the burden to establishing a genuine logical incompatibility.
Atkins's contention that suffering and innocent evil count against the existence of an all-loving God.
Craig distinguishes coexistence from contradiction, supplies a possible morally sufficient reason, and argues that this defeats the alleged logical incompatibility.
The universe cannot arise from nothing, and Atkins's zero-energy account neither eliminates existing things nor removes the need for a transcendent cause.
This extended defense supplies the causal bridge from a cosmic beginning to a transcendent cause, one of Craig's principal reasons for theism.
Atkins's claim that science may explain cosmic origins and that balanced positive and negative energy reduces reality to nothing.
Craig argues that nothing has no causal powers, rejects the inference from net-zero energy to nonexistence, and derives a philosophical cause of the universe.
An infinite sequence of universes cannot be ruled out by philosophical examples about finite cosmic systems; the issue must be decided by evidence.
It challenges the key premise that the universe has an absolute beginning and disputes Craig's philosophical method for excluding an infinite past.
Craig's philosophical arguments that an actually infinite past is impossible and that the universe therefore began to exist.
Atkins separates the measured ages of our universe and solar system from a possible infinite succession of universes and demands empirical evidence.
Balancing positive mass-energy against gravitational energy simplifies the origin problem without implying that concrete things literally do not exist.
The argument repairs Atkins's central naturalistic account after Craig's criticism and explains why a net-zero universe need not require divine contribution.
Craig's criticism that Atkins inferred literal nonexistence from balanced positive and negative energy and thereby contradicted himself.
Atkins describes measuring matter and gravitational energy, says their balance may approach zero, and presents this as narrowing the scientific explanatory task.
Morality can emerge through evolution and reflection on social consequences, so moral conduct and understanding do not require a divine source.
It contests the proposition that God is the necessary transcendent foundation of morality and offers a naturalistic genealogy of moral behavior.
Craig's argument that objective moral values and duties cannot exist without God as their transcendent foundation.
Atkins objects that atheists can be moral, urges investigation of morality's evolutionary roots, and contrasts understanding with appeal to a divine umpire.
The resurrection lacks extraordinary evidence because the Gospel reports are late, partisan political constructions rather than reliable historical records.
It directly contests Craig's historical case for divine action by attacking the reliability and provenance of the sources supporting the resurrection.
Craig's claim that the empty tomb, postmortem appearances, and origin of Christian belief establish a resurrection best explained by God.
Atkins invokes the need for unusually strong evidence, portrays the Gospels as interested propaganda, and denies that the available record warrants resurrection belief.
Philosophical objections to an actual infinite and scientific evidence for a past spacetime boundary jointly support a personal transcendent cause of the universe.
This is Craig's consolidated defense of the cosmological route to the motion's transcendent personal cause, combining metaphysical and scientific premises.
Atkins's objections that infinity arguments are unreliable, an endless sequence of universes remains possible, and net-zero energy removes divine necessity.
Craig distinguishes mathematical from concrete infinity, appeals to a past spacetime boundary, rejects the zero-energy response, and restates the cause's divine attributes.
Evolutionary accounts cannot ground mind-independent moral validity, whereas objective moral experience points to God as its transcendent foundation.
The passage directly supports the motion's claim that God grounds objective morality and distinguishes moral behavior from the ontological basis of moral duties.
Atkins's response that atheists can live morally and that moral behavior can be explained through evolution and social reflection.
Craig denies arguing that atheists behave badly, contends evolution yields contingent preferences without objective validity, and appeals to experienced moral truths.
Once the relevant background evidence and comparative explanatory virtues are considered, divine resurrection is not intrinsically improbable and best explains the historical facts.
It defends Craig's principal historical evidence for divine action by answering the probability objection and comparing the resurrection with rival explanations.
Atkins's Humean contention that miracle reports are less credible than ordinary alternatives and that resurrection evidence is partisan and inadequate.
Craig argues that Hume neglects the probability of the evidence absent resurrection, distinguishes natural revival from divine action, and invokes explanatory comparison.
Craig's theistic claims rely on untestable faith rather than evidence and therefore do not provide genuine explanations or scientific understanding.
This challenges the evidential status of the entire affirmative case and presents empirical testability as the decisive standard separating naturalism from theism.
Craig's claim that science supports premises in philosophical arguments for God and that his case is not a conflict between science and religion.
Atkins characterizes Craig's explanations as faith-based assertions, contrasts them with cautious evidential inquiry, and denies that divine intentions yield comprehension.
The universe began to exist, science cannot explain being arising from non-being, and the beginning therefore supports a transcendent cause.
This restates and defends the cosmological argument, one of Craig's principal grounds for affirming the debate motion.
Atkins's claim that science is progressing toward an account of the universe without invoking God.
In his closing statement Craig distinguishes physical investigation of whether the past is finite from the metaphysical question of how being could arise from non-being.
Objective moral values and duties plausibly exist and require God as their transcendent foundation.
The proposition directly supports the motion's claim that God is the foundation of objective morality.
Craig argues that atheism leaves morality in sociocultural relativism while objective duties are more evident than skeptical premises used to deny them.
Atkins's comparison of resurrection appearances with Elvis sightings fails to explain the appearances and the empty tomb.
The move defends Craig's historical case for divine intervention by challenging the proposed naturalistic alternative explanation.
Atkins's contention that reports of seeing Jesus after death resemble posthumous sightings of Elvis.
Craig argues that lies and hallucinations do not fit the diverse resurrection appearances, would not produce Jewish resurrection belief, and leave the empty tomb unexplained.
Craig's logical, causal, and personal arguments lack evidential support and cannot establish God.
This is Atkins's consolidated closing attack on the main forms of reasoning offered in support of God's existence.
Craig's logical deductions, cosmological first-cause inference, resurrection case, and account of morality.
Atkins says logic cannot validate its own starting assertion, causal reasoning is extrapolated beyond the universe, and personal claims favor anecdote and authority over evidence.
Natural explanations remove the need for creator, designer, purposeful, loving, moral-umpire, or interventionist conceptions of God.
The enumeration directly denies both the need for God and several personal, moral, and interventionist attributes specified by the motion.
Atkins summarizes his case as eliminating multiple proposed functions of God through natural accounts of origins, design, purpose, morality, suffering, and alleged miracles.
Scientific inquiry is progressively achieving a complete understanding of reality, making the God explanation intellectually unnecessary.
This supplies Atkins's overarching naturalistic alternative to theism and expressly concludes that reality does not include God.
Craig's use of God as the explanatory conclusion for questions that scientific inquiry has not yet resolved.
Atkins imagines a scientifically advanced society treating a simple divine answer as empty, while collective evidence-based inquiry continues toward understanding everything that exists.
Science can support a religiously neutral premise in an argument with theological significance without functioning as a God-of-the-gaps appeal.
The move defends the methodological legitimacy of Craig's central cosmological reasoning against the charge that it opposes science.
Atkins's portrayal of Craig as a pessimistic philosopher who inserts theology wherever science lacks an answer.
Craig says scientific evidence bears on the neutral claim that the universe began, while philosophical reasoning may then place that premise in an argument with theological consequences.
Only observation and scientific theorizing reveal how the world works; philosophy contributes nothing to that empirical task.
This epistemological principle underwrites Atkins's rejection of metaphysical arguments for God and his preference for scientific naturalism.
Craig's defense of philosophical reasoning informed by scientific evidence as a route to theological conclusions.
Atkins grants a role for moral philosophy but maintains that understanding nature requires observations organized into theories and that philosophy adds nothing to science.
Causality is a metaphysical principle governing being itself, so the universe's beginning requires a transcendent cause rather than an antecedent physical law.
The response protects the key inference in Craig's cosmological argument from the objection that causality presupposes an existing universe.
Atkins's objection that causal laws depend on an existing universe and therefore cannot explain its beginning.
Craig denies that there was a prior time containing nothing, explains that time itself began, and argues that being can arise only from being under metaphysical causality.
Evolutionary social utility cannot create binding objective duties, so atheistic morality collapses into sociocultural relativism.
The move defends the moral-foundation component of the motion by arguing that naturalistic utility cannot ground objective obligation.
Atkins's claim that evolution produces objectively moral conduct by sustaining stable and flourishing human societies.
Craig grants that cooperative norms aid survival but argues that dissent then violates only local mores, leaving cultures without a transcendent standard by which one can be judged wrong.
